t: Apostle: sent with the sender's authority
p: Paul opens by claiming an authority that does not come from any human source.
b: The Greek apostolos means someone sent out with the full authority of the one who sends, like an envoy. In the churches it was used of the Twelve and of others commissioned by the risen Lord (1 Corinthians 15:5-9). Paul's opening is unusual: he adds two denials, 'not from people, and not through any human being.' This looks like an answer to a charge that his authority came from the Jerusalem apostles or from the church at Antioch, which would make it a copy of theirs and a lesser one (1:11-12, 17). Letters at the time began with a name and a title and little more. Paul's long opening is already a defense.

a: through Jesus Christ and God the Father
t: Jesus Christ and God the Father together
p: One 'through' covers both names, and God is described only as the one who raised Jesus.
b: The Greek has a single 'through' for both names, so Paul puts Jesus beside God as the source of his commission. The only thing he says about God here is that he 'raised him from the dead', a short way of saying who God is: the one who acted in Jesus (Romans 4:24; 8:11). The Galatians are being asked to remember that the good news began with that act, not with a human message.

t: Brothers: a family word for scolded readers
p: The Greek 'brothers' is the plural used for the whole group, women included.
b: The Greek is the plural adelphoi, 'brothers', and Greek used the masculine plural for a mixed group. It is the usual way the New Testament addresses a whole church, and Paul uses it in Galatians at 1:11; 3:15; 4:12, 28, 31; 5:11, 13; 6:1, 18. Many English versions now write 'brothers and sisters', and others keep 'brothers' as the Plain does, with a gloss, as in Acts and Romans. In a letter of rebuke the word does a job: however angry Paul is, they are still family.

p: North or South? Where the churches lay changes the date of the letter, not its argument.
b: 'Galatia' could mean the old northern region around Ancyra (modern Ankara), where Celtic tribes had settled in the 270s BC, or the Roman province of Galatia, which from 25 BC also took in Pisidia, Lycaonia and part of Phrygia in the south. North Galatian view: the churches were in the north, founded on the journeys of Acts 16:6 and 18:23, and the letter is from the mid-50s. South Galatian view: Paul used the provincial name, and the churches are those of Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe (Acts 13:14-14:23); the letter could then be as early as the late 40s. Acts never calls those southern towns 'Galatia'. See the chapter page.

p: Paul turns the Greek letter greeting into 'grace' and joins the Hebrew 'peace'. Then the thanks is missing.
b: Greek letters began with chairein, 'greetings'. Paul changes it to charis, 'grace', and joins shalom, Hebrew 'peace' (the same words open Romans 1:7). In his other letters a thanksgiving to God follows (Romans 1:8; 1 Corinthians 1:4). In Galatians it does not: the next thing is 'I am amazed.' 'Grace' becomes a key word of the letter (1:6, 15; 2:9, 21; 5:4).

a: He gave himself for our sins
t: A very early summary of the good news
p: This looks like a formula older than the letter, with an echo of the suffering servant.
b: Many scholars hear a short creed behind these words, like 'Christ died for our sins' in 1 Corinthians 15:3 and Romans 4:25. 'Gave himself' echoes the servant who 'emptied out his life... He bore the sin of many' (Isaiah 53:12), and Paul repeats it in 2:20. The Greek preposition is hyper, 'for, on behalf of'; some manuscripts, the Byzantine text among them, have peri, 'concerning'. The English hardly changes.

a: the evil age that is now with us
p: Paul sees history in two ages, and Christ's death as a rescue out of the old one.
b: Jewish writers of Paul's time spoke of 'this age' and 'the age to come' (for example 4 Ezra 7:50). Paul says Christ gave himself to take believers out of this age, which is already breaking up (compare 1 Corinthians 10:11; 2 Corinthians 5:17; Galatians 6:14-15). 'Is now with us' renders enestōs, 'set in place, present'. J. Louis Martyn built a reading of the whole letter on this verse: Galatians is about God's invasion of an evil world, not only about how an individual is made right. Others accept the apocalyptic edge but think it is less central.
orig: αἰὼν ὁ ἐνεστὼς πονηρός (aion ho enestos poneros)

t: 'I am amazed': a rebuke where thanks should be
p: Letters of rebuke in the Greek world often began this way, so the form already tells the readers how Paul feels.
b: Paul gives thanks for his readers at this point in nearly every other letter (Romans 1:8; 1 Corinthians 1:4; Philippians 1:3). Here he writes thaumazō, 'I am astonished'. Some scholars note that Greek letters of rebuke used this very opening, so that Paul may be choosing the genre of a rebuke deliberately. The omission is a sharp signal to a church that expected praise.

p: The verb is probably in the middle voice: the Galatians are doing the switching, and it is still in progress.
b: Metatithesthe means to change position, party or loyalty; Lightfoot gives examples of the verb used for leaving one philosophical school or party for another. It is present tense, so the change is happening now and can still be stopped (4:19-20; 5:10). The verb is probably middle voice (it could also be passive, 'being moved'), in which case they are turning themselves, not being carried off; which it is bears on how much of the blame Paul puts on them. Paul treats the matter as desertion of a person (the one who called them) before it is a change of teaching.

p: Paul uses two Greek words for 'other'; the point is that there is only one good news.
b: Verse 6 says heteron ('different') and verse 7 says allo ('another'). Lightfoot saw a difference of kind versus number; others think Paul is not making a fine distinction. Either way the logic is the same: there is only one good news, so what the agitators offer is not a rival version of it but a twisting of it. 'Good news' is euangelion, the word behind 'gospel'.

a: some people who are upsetting you
p: Paul never names the people he is fighting; scholars rebuild who they were from his replies.
b: The verb tarassō means to stir up, throw into confusion. Paul gives no names and says they will 'pay the penalty, whoever they are' (5:10). From his answers scholars rebuild a picture; the method is called mirror-reading and is risky, since Paul's replies may not match what the agitators said. Views: Jewish Christians from Jerusalem or Judea who held that Gentile believers must become proselytes (the traditional 'Judaizers'; compare Acts 15:1, 5), the most common view; Gentile Christians drawn to the law; or Jewish teachers outside the Christian groups who pressed Gentile followers of Christ to be circumcised so that the synagogues would accept them (Mark Nanos).

t: Anathema: handed over to God's judgment
p: A curse formula from the Greek Old Testament, used here on anyone who preaches another good news.
b: Anathema in the Greek Old Testament translates Hebrew herem, the ban: something devoted to God for destruction (Deuteronomy 7:26; Joshua 6:17-18). Paul uses it of his own wish in Romans 9:3 and in 1 Corinthians 16:22 ('if anyone does not love the Lord, let him be anathema'). Here the curse falls on anyone, even Paul, who changes the good news: the boundary is the message, not a person. Betz notes that this curse matches the blessing in 6:16, so the letter is framed by them. Later councils took the word as a formula for excluding someone from the church.

p: An angel is the highest authority Paul can think of, and still he says no.
b: The angel is a rhetorical extreme: no messenger, however high, can change the message. Angels come back in 3:19, where the law was arranged 'through angels', and some commentators wonder whether the agitators appealed to angelic authority for the law. Later Christians have used this verse as a test for claimed new revelations; the groups concerned reject the application. Paul's own point is only that the good news he had already given is the measure of every later claim, including his own.

t: When did he say it before?
p: Paul moves from 'we' to 'I' and adds 'right now, again': the curse is now in his own voice.
b: The Plain keeps the plural 'we have said before' (proeirēkamen), then the singular 'I say again right now' (arti palin legō). The plural may look back to Paul's earlier visit (or visits) to Galatia, or to the sentence just written in verse 8. The plural 'we' of verse 8 (Paul and his companions) becomes 'I' here, a change that makes the curse personal. A repeat is a rhetorical choice: in a speech, a point said twice is meant to be remembered.

t: 'Win people over': a charge of people-pleasing?
p: Paul may be answering the charge that he bent his message to suit his hearers.
b: Peithō means to persuade, to win over. Critics may have said that Paul preached a law-free good news to Gentiles to make it easy, while keeping the law when he was among Jews (compare Acts 16:3, where he circumcises Timothy, and 1 Corinthians 9:19-23, 'to the Jews I became like a Jew'). Paul answers that a servant of Christ cannot be a people-pleaser. A later verse suggests the charge of inconsistency was real: 'If I still preach circumcision, why am I still persecuted?' (5:11).

p: 'Slave' was a low status and also, in Scripture, a title of honor.
b: A slave in the Roman world was the property of his master and had no will of his own. But 'slave (servant) of the LORD' was also a title of honor for Moses, David and the prophets. Paul uses 'slave of Christ' in the openings of Romans 1:1 and Philippians 1:1; here the word stands against people-pleasing, since a slave serves one master. See the note on 'slave' at Romans 1:1.

p: Paul claims that his message is not of human kind or origin.
b: The Greek kata anthrōpon, 'according to man', can mean human in measure, in kind or in origin. Paul uses it again at 3:15 ('in human terms') and Romans 3:5. The claim is not that Paul invented nothing, since he hands on what he received (1 Corinthians 15:3), but that the source and the shape of the good news is God's act in Christ, not human reasoning. He explains in the next verse how he received it.

p: Paul's call: a revelation that Jesus gave, or one whose content is Jesus? The Greek allows both.
b: The genitive 'of Jesus Christ' can mean a revelation given by Jesus (subjective) or a revelation whose content is Jesus (objective). Verse 16, 'to reveal his Son in me', favors the second. Acts tells the story three times, with a light and a voice (Acts 9:3-6; 22:6-10; 26:12-18). Acts 9:3: 'He was on the road and nearing Damascus when all at once light from heaven flashed all around him.' Paul himself says only that he saw the Lord (1 Corinthians 9:1; 15:8). What mattered for him was the source: God, not a human teacher.

t: 'Judaism': Paul's first word for his old life
p: The word first appears in 2 Maccabees; it means loyalty to the Jewish way of life, not 'a religion' as we use the word.
b: Ioudaismos first appears in 2 Maccabees (2:21; 8:1; 14:38) as the opposite of Hellenismos, the Greek way: it names active, even militant loyalty to the Jewish way of life and the covenant. Paul uses it only here and in 1:14. 'Former life in Judaism' does not settle whether he thinks he left it: Paul-within-Judaism readers (Nanos, Eisenbaum, Fredriksen) say he moved within it, as a Jew who now believed in Christ; others say he had broken with it. The Plain says 'when I was in Judaism'.

p: Paul says he persecuted 'beyond all measure'; the reasons are debated.
b: The persecution is told in Acts 8:3; 9:1-2; 22:4-5; 26:9-11 and mentioned in 1 Corinthians 15:9 and Philippians 3:6. Why? Views: the Hellenist believers around Stephen seemed to speak against the Temple and the law (Acts 6:13-14); the claim that a man executed on a tree was Messiah offended Deuteronomy 21:23 (see 3:13); and the movement was taking in Gentiles without circumcision. Zeal that used force to guard Israel's holiness had models in Phinehas and Mattathias (1 Maccabees 2:26). 'Church of God' means God's assembly, a name taken from Israel's gathering in the wilderness.
r: Acts 8:3; Acts 9:1-2; 1 Corinthians 15:9; Philippians 3:6; Deuteronomy 21:23; 1 Maccabees 2:26

p: Paul's training in the traditions fits what Acts and Josephus say about the Pharisees.
b: Paul calls himself a Pharisee (Philippians 3:5), a student of Gamaliel in Jerusalem (Acts 22:3), and one who 'lived as a Pharisee, following the most exacting party of our religion' (Acts 26:5). Josephus says the Pharisees passed on to the people many rules 'from the fathers' that are not in the law of Moses (Antiquities 13.297). Jesus speaks of the 'tradition of the elders' (Mark 7:3-5). For Paul, zeal for such traditions showed itself in the persecution of 1:13; later he counts it loss for Christ (Philippians 3:7).

a: set me apart from the womb of my mother
p: Paul describes his call in the words of Jeremiah and of the Servant in Isaiah.
b: Jeremiah heard: "I gave you to the nations as a prophet" (Jeremiah 1:5). The Servant says: "The LORD called me from the womb" (Isaiah 49:1), and is made 'a light to the nations' (Isaiah 49:6). Paul quotes neither, but 'set apart from the womb', 'called' and 'to the Gentiles' (1:16) are a close echo. Krister Stendahl argued that Paul was not converted from one religion to another but called, like a prophet, to a task, and the Plain follows him in saying 'call'. Others keep the word 'conversion' for the great change from persecutor to apostle.

p: Most versions say 'to me'; the Greek says 'in me'.
b: En emoi is literally 'in me'. Several scholars hear more than 'to me': God revealed his Son inwardly, in Paul's life, so that Paul could then make him known to others. Acts stresses an outward event (a light, a voice); Paul links the experience with 'Christ is alive in me' (2:20). The Plain keeps the Greek 'in me' and leaves the choice to the reader.

t: Called to the nations from the start
p: Paul says that his call and his task came together.
b: Paul ties the revelation of the Son to the task of telling the good news 'among the Gentiles' (Greek ethnē, 'the nations'). Acts says the same of the Damascus call (Acts 9:15; 22:21; 26:17-18). The prophets had foretold that the nations would turn to the God of Israel (Isaiah 49:6: "I will give you as a light to the nations"), and Paul sees himself inside that promise (Romans 15:9-12). Paul-within-Judaism scholars (Fredriksen, Gager) stress that his mission was to non-Jews as non-Jews: he did not set out to make Gentiles into Jews.

p: A Jewish expression for ordinary human beings, as against God.
b: 'Flesh and blood' is a Jewish way of saying human beings, weak and mortal, in contrast with God (Sirach 14:18; Matthew 16:17; 1 Corinthians 15:50; Ephesians 6:12). 'Talk it over' translates prosanethemēn (from prosanatithemai), to lay a matter before someone for explanation or approval. Paul says he did not rush to check his experience with anyone. In 2:2 he does lay his preaching before the Jerusalem leaders, but 'after fourteen years' and for a different reason.

a: men who had been apostles before me
t: 'Before me': first in time, not higher in rank
p: Paul names the Jerusalem apostles as his predecessors and insists he did not need their approval.
b: 'Before me' says who came first, not who ranks above. In 1 Corinthians 15:5-9 Paul lists those the risen Lord appeared to, himself 'last of all', and calls himself the least of the apostles. His claim in Galatians is independence, not rivalry: the Jerusalem apostles really were apostles before him, and his commission did not pass through them.

p: He does not say what he did there, and Acts does not mention the trip.
b: In Paul's time 'Arabia' usually meant the kingdom of the Nabateans, which reached from the Negev through Transjordan and included land near Damascus. Its king Aretas IV had a governor in Damascus when Paul escaped through a window in the wall (2 Corinthians 11:32-33; compare Acts 9:23-25). Views: Paul preached in Nabatean territory and stirred up the authorities (Hengel and Schwemer); he went into the desert to pray and rethink, perhaps to Mount Sinai, where Elijah had gone (1 Kings 19:8; Paul puts Sinai 'in Arabia' at Galatians 4:25); or both. The 'three years' of 1:18 include this time.

p: Cephas is the Aramaic word for 'rock'; Peter is the Greek form.
b: Kēphas is Aramaic Kepha, 'rock'; Petros is its Greek form. John 1:42 says Jesus gave Simon the name Cephas. Paul uses 'Cephas' in Galatians 1:18; 2:9, 11, 14 and in 1 Corinthians, and 'Peter' only at 2:7-8. The Byzantine text and the KJV's Greek replace 'Cephas' with 'Peter' at 1:18, 2:11 and 2:14, which hides Paul's own usage. Eusebius (Church History 1.12) quotes Clement of Alexandria's Hypotyposes as saying that the Cephas of Galatians 2:11 was a different man, one of the Seventy disciples; almost no one holds that now.

p: The Greek verb behind 'history' can mean to visit, to get to know, or to question.
b: Historēsai (from which English gets 'history') means to inquire, look into, get to know a person or a place. Lightfoot calls the verb 'somewhat emphatic' and quotes Chrysostom, who said it is used of people who go to see great and famous cities, so that it suggests a visit to someone worth seeing; others say it means no more than 'visit a person of importance'. Whatever Paul learned, his point is the length of the stay: fifteen days with one man is not a course of instruction, and he saw no other apostle but James. The Plain says 'to meet', a neutral word.

t: Fifteen days, and the story in Acts
p: Acts tells the same visit with different details; the two can be put together.
b: Acts 9:26-29 tells of Saul's first visit to Jerusalem after Damascus: the disciples feared him, "Barnabas, however, took hold of Saul and led him to the apostles" (Acts 9:27), and then he spoke boldly until Greek-speaking Jews tried to kill him and the brothers sent him to Tarsus. Paul says nothing of Barnabas or a plot, and names only Cephas and James. A common way to put them together is that 'the apostles' of Acts 9:27 means Cephas and James alone. Paul's 'I am not lying' in 1:20 shows that the facts of his visits were being questioned.

a: James, the brother of the Lord
t: James, the brother of the Lord
p: Was James a full brother, a half-brother or a cousin of Jesus? The churches answer differently.
b: James led the Jerusalem church (Acts 12:17; 15:13; 21:18; Galatians 2:9, 12). Three views of 'brother': younger brother, a son of Mary and Joseph born after Jesus, so a half-brother of Jesus (Helvidius, late 300s; the usual view among Protestants today; Mark 6:3); stepbrother, a son of Joseph by an earlier wife (the Eastern and Orthodox tradition); cousin, the son of another Mary (Jerome, about 383; the Catholic tradition). The grammar also matters: in 'except James', is James counted as an apostle? Many say yes (compare 1 Corinthians 15:7); others take 'except' to apply only to 'saw no one'. See the card.
r: Mark 6:3; Matthew 13:55; Acts 12:17; Acts 15:13; 1 Corinthians 15:7; Galatians 2:9

a: before God, I am not lying
p: Paul swears in the middle of a factual report, which shows the report was being doubted.
b: Paul uses oath language in Romans 9:1, 2 Corinthians 1:23; 11:31 and Philippians 1:8. Such oaths were not rare in Greek letters, but this one comes in the middle of a plain report of travel, which suggests that his account of his visits was under attack: perhaps that he had received his message from Jerusalem and then changed it. Betz reads the whole of Galatians as a courtroom speech, in which an oath is a natural way to back a claim.

p: Acts passes over these years in a few lines; Paul gives them one verse.
b: Cilicia was Paul's home province (Tarsus, Acts 9:30; 21:39; 22:3), and Antioch was the capital of Syria. Acts covers these years in a few lines: Paul goes to Tarsus (Acts 9:30), and Barnabas brings him to Antioch (Acts 11:25-26). Paul probably worked as a preacher among Jews and Gentiles. Some of the sufferings he lists in 2 Corinthians 11:24-27 (five times the thirty-nine lashes, shipwrecks) are not in Acts and may belong here. Hengel and Schwemer call these 'the unknown years' between Damascus and Antioch.

a: did not know me by sight
t: Judea did not know Paul's face
p: Paul separates 'the churches of Judea' from the Jerusalem apostles he had met.
b: Paul says the Judean churches knew him only by report (1:23). This sits uneasily with Acts 9:28, 'He was with them, coming and going in Jerusalem', unless Jerusalem is distinguished from the countryside of Judea, or Acts is more generous than Paul's fifteen days. 'In Christ' is Paul's phrase for belonging to the Messiah and his people (3:26-28). Paul's point is that he was not known, and so not taught, by the Judean churches.

p: 'The faith' can mean what is believed and preached, not only trust.
b: Here pistis with the article names the message or way of life of the believers: what the persecutor once tried to wreck and now announces as good news. Paul uses it the same way at 3:23, 25 ('this faith') and 6:10 ('the household of faith'). It is not only inward trust but also the thing believed, preached and lived. The Plain keeps 'the faith' and the reader should watch the context in each use.

p: Counted from his call or from the first visit? The answer shapes Paul's whole chronology.
b: Paul says 'then after fourteen years' following the 'three years' of 1:18. Some count from the first visit (so, with the three years, seventeen from his call); others count from his call, with the three years inside the fourteen. Ancient counting included part-years, so the numbers are loose. If Paul's call was about AD 31-36, the second visit falls in the AD 40s or early 50s by this count. The Gallio inscription at Delphi dates Gallio's time as governor at Corinth (Acts 18:12) to about AD 51-52 and is the anchor for dating Paul's later letters. See the chapter page for how this visit fits Acts.

p: A Levite from Cyprus who brought Paul into the Antioch church and travelled with him.
b: Barnabas, called Joseph, a Levite from Cyprus, sold a field for the Jerusalem church (Acts 4:36-37), brought Saul to the apostles (Acts 9:27), fetched him from Tarsus to Antioch (Acts 11:25-26) and led the first mission with him (Acts 13-14). Paul names him as his partner at the Jerusalem meeting (2:9) and as the one who was carried away at Antioch (2:13). Acts 15:36-40 shows the two parting over John Mark.
r: Acts 4:36-37; Acts 9:27; Acts 11:25-26; Acts 15:36-40; Galatians 2:9; Galatians 2:13

p: A Gentile co-worker whom Paul brought to Jerusalem to see what would be asked of him.
b: Titus is not named in Acts. Paul names him here and in 2 Corinthians, where he is Paul's envoy to Corinth (2 Corinthians 8:16-17, 23). Taking an uncircumcised Greek believer to Jerusalem in plain view of the leaders was a deliberate test: would Jerusalem require his circumcision? In Paul's account it did not (2:3).

p: Acts says the church sent Paul; Paul says a revelation sent him. The two can go together.
b: Acts says the church at Antioch sent Paul and Barnabas up to Jerusalem (Acts 15:2) or, in the famine visit, to carry relief (Acts 11:30). Paul says he went 'in answer to a revelation'. This may be a prophetic word, like that of the prophet Agabus, who "indicated through the Spirit that a great famine was going to strike the whole inhabited world" (Acts 11:28), or a private vision. A church can send delegates because of a prophecy. For Paul the point is that Jerusalem did not summon him: God sent him.

a: those who were held in high esteem
p: Paul's phrase is respectful on the surface and cool underneath.
b: Hoi dokountes, 'those who seem (to be something), the reputed ones', occurs in 2:2, 6 (twice) and 9. It can be neutral or honorific, but in 2:6 Paul adds 'whatever they once were makes no difference to me', which sounds dismissive. Commentators differ: some hear irony about the Jerusalem leaders; others hear respect for their real standing joined to a refusal to let rank settle the truth. The Plain keeps the same ambiguity.

a: running, or had run, for nothing
p: Paul sees his work as a race, and fears a split that would waste it.
b: Paul often pictures his work as a race (1 Corinthians 9:24-27; Philippians 2:16; 3:14). 'For nothing' (eis kenon) recalls the Servant's complaint in Isaiah 49:4 in the Greek Bible. Paul does not doubt his message, which he already knows is from God (1:12); he fears that a break with Jerusalem would make the mission fruitless, with a Jewish church and a Gentile church who could not eat at one table. That is the very worry that shows up at Antioch (2:11-14).

a: not even he was made to get circumcised
p: Circumcision was the sign of Abraham's covenant; the demand to circumcise Gentiles is the heart of the crisis.
b: Genesis 17:10 sets the rule: "every male among you is to be circumcised." To be circumcised made a Gentile a member of the Jewish people. Acts 15:1, 5 shows believers demanding it of Gentiles. Paul presents the case of Titus as proof that the Jerusalem leaders did not require it. Whether Titus was in fact circumcised under pressure is argued because of a textual variant at 2:5; the plain reading, followed by the Plain, is that he was not. Acts 16:3 says Paul circumcised Timothy: "So he took Timothy and circumcised him, on account of the Jews living in that area, since everyone knew his father was Greek." The cases differ: Timothy's mother was Jewish, and nobody was demanding it as a condition of his acceptance.

p: Paul seems to have made up the word; they presented themselves as believers.
b: Pseudadelphoi appears in Paul only here and in 2 Corinthians 11:26. They were 'brothers' in the community's eyes, 'false' in Paul's. Acts 15:5 describes the people he probably means: "Then some from the Pharisees' party who had become believers rose to their feet." 'Slipped in' and 'sneaked in' are the language of infiltration, and the details of when and where are unclear; it is Paul's side of the story, told with heat. Whether these are the same people as the agitators in Galatia (1:7) is not stated.

a: our freedom, which we hold in Christ Jesus
t: Freedom: the key word of Galatians
p: 'Freedom' opens the argument here and returns at 5:1 and 5:13.
b: Eleutheria is set against slavery throughout the letter (2:4; 4:3, 9, 24-25; 5:1). Paul's freedom is not freedom to do anything, since he calls himself Christ's slave (1:10) and tells the Galatians to serve one another in love (5:13). The Exodus is the Bible's pattern for freedom: God brought Israel out of slavery (Exodus 20:2). Freedom 'in Christ Jesus' is freedom from the evil age (1:4) and, for Gentile believers, from being made to keep Jewish law in order to belong.

p: Paul's phrase names what was at stake, at Jerusalem here and at Antioch in 2:14.
b: In 2:5 and 2:14 Paul speaks of 'the truth of the good news' as the thing he guards. He does not mean a list of statements. He means the way the good news works: if Gentiles must add circumcision to faith in Christ to be accepted, then Christ is not enough, and the good news is no longer the whole truth (compare 5:2-4). So he will not 'give way in submission' even for an hour. The same measure is used against Cephas.

a: does not go by a person's face
p: A Hebrew idiom for favoritism: God does not judge by status.
b: The idiom is the Hebrew nasa panim, 'lift the face', meaning to show favor to someone because of who he is (Deuteronomy 10:17; 2 Chronicles 19:7; Leviticus 19:15). It is in the Greek New Testament in Acts 10:34 and Romans 2:11. Paul uses it to say that the Jerusalem leaders' reputation does not decide the truth of his message: God does not rank people. The Plain keeps the picture, and a gloss gives the sense 'shows no favorites'.

p: Paul says nothing was added; Acts reports a letter with four requirements for Gentiles.
b: 'Added' is the verb prosanatithemai of 1:16. Paul means the leaders gave him no new teaching and no new requirements: no circumcision for Titus and no change to his message. Acts 15:29 reports a letter asking Gentile believers to "keep away from food sacrificed to idols, from blood, from what is strangled and from sexual sin." Paul never mentions this decree in Galatians. Those who put Galatians before the Council (see the chapter page) say it did not yet exist; others say Paul did not need it for this argument, or that the Council came later than the meeting he describes.

a: the good news for the uncircumcised
p: Paul and Peter had two mission fields, not two different messages.
b: The Greek has 'the good news of the uncircumcision' and 'of the circumcision'. Most scholars say this describes two audiences and two fields, not two messages, since Paul has just said there is only one good news (1:6-9). A few in the 1800s (F. C. Baur) saw two rival gospels. Paul-within-Judaism scholars (Gager, Eisenbaum, Nanos) hold that Jewish believers went on keeping the Torah, and that Paul's task was to bring Gentiles into God's family as Gentiles, which is the same Jesus message in two settings. The division was not strict: Paul preached first in synagogues (Acts 13:5), and Peter went to the household of Cornelius (Acts 10).

p: A pillar holds a building up; the picture is of the church as a house or temple.
b: The image appears in 1 Corinthians 3:9-16, Ephesians 2:20-22 and Revelation 3:12 (a pillar in the temple of God). 1 Clement 5:2 says that 'the greatest and most righteous pillars' of the church were persecuted, meaning Peter and Paul. Paul's words are 'those counted as pillars', which may be what the Jerusalem group called themselves; he writes with the same reserve as in 2:6. Matthew 16:18 calls Peter the rock on which the church is built; Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant readers differ on that.

p: Giving the right hand sealed an agreement; the word is koinonia, 'partnership'.
b: Giving the right hand was a sign of a pledge. The word koinōnia, 'partnership, sharing', is the word Paul later uses for the collection (Romans 15:26). James, Cephas and John recognized that God had given Paul the grace for the Gentile mission. Whether the division was by ethnicity or by geography is debated, and the agreement did not say how Jewish and Gentile believers would eat together, which is the problem of 2:11-14.

p: Paul kept this promise by gathering gifts from the Gentile churches for Jerusalem.
b: 'The poor' may be the poor of Jerusalem in general or the believers there (Romans 15:26, 'the poor among the saints'). Paul's collections from his Gentile churches are his way of keeping the promise: 1 Corinthians 16:1-4 (which says he gave the same order 'to the churches of Galatia'), 2 Corinthians 8-9, and Romans 15:25-31. Acts mentions relief sent from Antioch (Acts 11:29-30) and a gift Paul brought to Jerusalem (Acts 24:17). The gifts also expressed the partnership: the Gentiles owed a debt to those who had shared their spiritual blessings (Romans 15:27).

t: Antioch, third city of the empire
p: The clash happened in the mixed church of Antioch; its date is debated.
b: Antioch on the Orontes was the capital of Syria and one of the three greatest cities of the empire, with a large Jewish community (Josephus, Jewish War 7.43-45). Its church began among Hellenist believers scattered after Stephen (Acts 11:19-21) and sent out Paul and Barnabas (Acts 13:1-3). When did the incident happen? Many place it after the Jerusalem meeting of 2:1-10, since Barnabas is still Paul's partner there; others place it before the Council of Acts 15 and think it helped cause the Council. Paul tells it as the last case in his argument.

p: The Greek says only 'he stood condemned'; it does not say who condemned him.
b: Kategnōsmenos means 'condemned, found guilty'. By whom? By God (by the gospel's own standard), by his own action (his conduct contradicted what he believed), or by the Gentile believers whom he had slighted. The Plain says 'under condemnation' and leaves the agent open. What is clear is that Paul thinks Cephas' behavior contradicted Cephas' own convictions, as 2:12 and 2:14 explain.

p: Were they sent by James, or only from his circle? Paul does not say.
b: Paul does not call these people 'false brothers' here. Were they sent by James with a message, or did they only come from the Jerusalem church and use his name? Acts 15:24 shows Jerusalem disowning people who came from them: "We gave them no orders." That may or may not be the same event. Jewett suggested that James and the Jerusalem church were under pressure from zealous Jews in Judea and urged Jewish believers elsewhere to be careful about their reputation, which would explain Cephas' fear.

a: he used to eat with the Gentiles
t: What was wrong with eating together?
p: Meals were the sign of full acceptance; for Jews, Gentile tables raised questions of food, purity and idols.
b: Jews could eat with Gentiles, but there were problems: food not prepared by Torah rules, meat or wine tied to idol offerings, and ritual impurity. Views on the issue at Antioch: Torah food laws and purity (Dunn); idolatry, since sharing the wine might let Gentiles turn it into a pagan libation (Esler); how Jews and Gentiles were seated together (Nanos); or table fellowship itself as the sign that Gentiles were equal members, which Cephas' withdrawal denied. Peter had been criticized for eating with Gentiles before: "You went in among uncircumcised men" (Acts 11:3). See Acts 10:28.

p: Jews generally, Jewish believers, or non-believing Jews who could cause trouble?
b: Paul writes 'fearing those of the circumcision', which suggests outsiders who could cause trouble. Robert Jewett argued that nationalist pressure in Judea in the 40s led Jewish Christians to press Gentile converts to be circumcised, so that the Christian groups would not look lax to zealots. Paul says something similar of the agitators in 6:12: they want 'to avoid being persecuted for the cross of Christ'.

p: The Greek word is from the theater: playing a part that hides what you think.
b: The Greek hypokritēs was a stage actor, and hypokrisis is playing a part, so 'hypocrisy' means acting in a way that hides one's real conviction. Paul's charge is not that Cephas was a bad man but that he acted against what he knew. Jesus used the word of play-acting piety (Matthew 23:28). Barnabas, Paul's partner in the Gentile mission, 'was carried away' (the Greek verb has the sense of being swept off by a current).

p: A word found nowhere else in the New Testament.
b: Orthopodeō is literally 'to walk with straight feet'. It can mean to walk straight toward a goal, to be on the right foot, or to be in step. The Latin Vulgate has non recte ambularent, 'they were not walking rightly'. Paul measures Cephas by the 'truth of the good news' (2:5), not by tradition or rank. 'Walk' is Paul's usual picture for conduct (5:16, 25).

p: The Greek has no quotation marks; Bibles end Paul's words to Cephas in different places.
b: Some English Bibles close Paul's words to Cephas after 2:14; others run them through 2:21; a few end at 2:16 or 2:18. The Plain closes them at the end of 2:14, since 2:15 begins 'We ourselves are Jews by nature' and turns to the Galatians as well as Cephas. Either way, 2:15-21 is Paul's statement to the Galatians of what he believes. Paul does not say how Cephas answered, and the silence has been read as Paul's victory or as a sign that the matter was not settled.

p: Paul rebukes Cephas in front of the whole assembly; later readers disagreed about what to make of that.
b: Matthew 18:15-17 recommends private correction first, but Paul says the fault was public, since Cephas' conduct had shaped the whole community. Aquinas used this verse to teach that a subordinate may correct a superior in public when the faith is in danger (Summa II-II, q. 33, art. 4). Origen (as Jerome reports), Jerome and Chrysostom thought the quarrel was staged for the Gentiles' benefit, and Augustine rejected that view. See the card at 2:11-14.

p: The verb means to live as Jews do, including keeping Jewish food and circumcision rules.
b: Ioudaïzein means to adopt Jewish customs. It is used in Josephus of an officer who offered to 'Judaize', even to the point of circumcision, to save his life (Jewish War 2.454), and in the Greek version of Esther 8:17 of Gentiles who were circumcised and 'became Jews'. Paul's charge is that Cephas' withdrawal pressed Gentiles to adopt Jewish practice to be accepted at table. The English word 'Judaizers' comes from this verse; it appears nowhere else in the New Testament.

p: 'By nature' means by birth: Paul starts from what Jewish believers all agree on.
b: Here physei means 'by birth', one's origin (as in Romans 2:27). Paul speaks as a Jewish believer to Jewish believers, Cephas and Barnabas, before he turns to the Galatians in 2:16. He begins from common ground: even those born into the covenant know that being right with God does not come by the works of the law.

p: 'Sinner' was a Jewish way of speaking about Gentiles, and Paul says it with a sting.
b: In Jewish speech of the time 'sinner' and 'Gentile' overlapped: compare Matthew 5:47 with Luke 6:33, where Matthew's 'Gentiles' are Luke's 'sinners', and 1 Maccabees 2:44, where 'sinners' are lawless Jews who side with the nations. Some scholars read Paul's phrase as an ironic quotation of this idea. In 2:17 Paul will say that Jewish believers who eat with Gentiles are also 'found to be sinners'.

p: Does Paul mean every deed the law asks, or the practices that marked Jews off from others?
b: The phrase occurs three times in this verse, then in 3:2, 5, 10 and Romans 3:20, 28. Views: all deeds the law commands, which no one keeps perfectly (Luther, Calvin; Moo, Schreiner); the practices that marked Jews off from Gentiles, circumcision, Sabbath and food laws (James Dunn and N. T. Wright, the New Perspective); and the Catholic teaching that no works of human strength or of the law justify without grace, while works done in grace belong to the Christian life (Trent, session 6). The Dead Sea text 4QMMT, 'Some of the Works of the Torah' (a sectarian letter, dated by its editors to about 150 BC), has the Hebrew phrase in its title, and Martin Abegg reads it as saying that keeping its rules 'will be accounted to you as righteousness'. The Plain keeps 'works of the law' so that every use can be compared.

p: The Greek 'unless, except' seems to let works in, but the rest of the verse shuts them out.
b: Ean mē usually means 'unless, except'. Read that way, Paul might seem to say that works of the law do justify when they are joined to faith. Burton argues that the exception applies only to 'a person is not justified', not to 'by works of the law': a person is not justified, except through faith in Christ. The rest of the verse makes this clear ('by faith in Christ and not by works of the law'). The Plain keeps 'except' to show the Greek form.

p: The verb comes from the same root as 'righteous'; the churches read it differently.
b: Dikaioō is a law-court word in the Greek Bible: the judge declares someone in the right (Exodus 23:7; Deuteronomy 25:1; Psalm 143:2). Protestants stress the declaration, based on Christ's work and received by faith; Catholic teaching includes the renewal of the person (Trent, session 6); the Orthodox stress healing and union with God. The New Perspective stresses that 'justified' says who belongs to God's family, here in a dispute about who may eat together (2:11-14). The Plain uses 'justify' with a gloss, as in Romans.
r: Exodus 23:7; Deuteronomy 25:1; Psalm 143:2; Romans 3:20; Romans 3:28; Romans 5:1

p: Paul takes the psalmist's 'no living person' and adds 'by works of the law'.
b: The last clause echoes Psalm 143:2: "for no living person is in the right in your presence." Paul writes 'no flesh' (the Greek Psalm has 'no one living') and adds 'by works of the law'. The same echo is in Romans 3:20. 'Flesh' means a human being in his weakness. Whether the addition is Paul's reading of what the psalm already implies, that no human effort suffices, or his sharpening of it for the Gentile question, is debated.

p: Paul's exclamation of refusal, used 14 times in his letters.
b: Mē genoito, literally 'may it not happen', is a sharp denial. Paul uses it 14 times, ten of them in Romans, in the style of the diatribe, where a teacher answers an imaginary opponent. The Plain writes 'By no means!' as in Romans (see Romans 6:2) and not the older 'God forbid', which adds a word Paul does not use.

t: Is Christ a servant of sin?
p: Paul answers an objection; what the objection is depends on how verses 15-18 are read.
b: Views. (1) The objection is about Antioch: if Jewish believers eat with Gentiles and so live in the Gentile way (2:14), they become 'sinners' by the Torah's standard, so is Christ the servant of sin? (2) It is about moral failure after justification: if believers still sin, is Christ to blame? (Luther's reading). (3) Lightfoot weighs two readings, an objection from Judaizers and Paul's own argument, and prefers neither: he takes the clause as an illogical conclusion drawn from a true premise. To be justified in Christ, believers had to give up legal righteousness and stand where Gentiles stood, 'sinners' from a Jewish point of view; does it follow that Christ is a servant of sin? In every reading Paul's answer is that the sin is in rebuilding the wall that Christ took down (2:18).

p: Paul speaks as 'I' but is describing any Jewish Christian who goes back.
b: Parabatēs is one who steps over a line, a transgressor (Romans 2:25, 27). The 'I' is a rhetorical I standing for any Jewish believer, as in Romans 7. 'The things I pulled down' are probably the barriers of the law in the sense of 2:14-15 or the law as the way to righteousness (Luther). To build them again is to say that the law was right after all, which would make the earlier 'tearing down' a sin: by Paul's own standard, a lawbreaker.

a: through the law, died to the law
t: Died to the law through the law
p: Three readings of how the law led Paul to die to the law.
b: (1) The law itself, by condemning him, brought Paul to give up on it (Luther; compare Romans 7:9-11). (2) The law's own witness to Christ (Romans 3:21) led him to leave the law as a way of life. In every case 2:20, 'crucified together with Christ', is the explanation.

p: A perfect tense: the crucifixion happened and its result stays.
b: The Greek perfect tense says that Paul was crucified with Christ and that this stands. Paul returns to it in 6:14 ('the world has been crucified to me'). Dying and rising with Christ is also in Romans 6:3-6. E. P. Sanders called Paul's language of being in Christ and with Christ 'participation'. Michael Gorman calls the pattern 'cruciformity': life shaped by Christ's cross. The Plain keeps 'together with' to show the preposition syn.

p: Here 'flesh' means ordinary bodily life, not sinful desire.
b: Paul can live 'in the flesh' and yet 'by faith' (compare Philippians 1:22, 24; 2 Corinthians 10:3, 'we live in the flesh' but do not fight 'according to the flesh'). Here the word means the body and its ordinary life, which Paul does not despise. 'Flesh' takes a darker sense in 3:3 and 5:16-17, where it stands against the Spirit. The Plain keeps 'flesh' throughout so that readers can follow the word from place to place.

t: 'Loved me and gave himself up for me'
p: Paul takes the creed of 1:4 and makes it personal.
b: 'Giving up' language appears at 1:4, in Romans 8:32 and Ephesians 5:2, 25, and echoes the Servant who was 'handed over' for our sins in the Greek Isaiah 53:12. 'Me' is striking, since Paul had persecuted the church (1:13). Luther's 1531 lectures stress the personal pronoun: faith believes that it is for me. Later readers have contrasted this with the 'for us' of 1:4 and 3:13. The words just before, 'I live it by faith in the Son of God' (Greek en pistei zō tē tou huiou tou theou, literally 'in the faith of the Son of God'), raise the same question as 2:16: faith in the Son, or the Son's own faithfulness. The following clause, 'who loved me and gave himself up for me', fits either. See the variant and the note at 3:22.

p: To make the law the way to righteousness would void grace.
b: Atheteō means to set aside, make void, reject. The same verb is used of a human covenant at 3:15, where the Plain says 'cancels'. Paul's last charge is that making the law the way to righteousness makes grace unnecessary. This is where the argument of 2:11-21 lands.

t: 'For no reason': the same word as 'freely'
p: The Greek adverb that means 'freely' in Romans 3:24 here means 'without cause'.
b: Dōrean is the word of Romans 3:24 ('justified freely, by his grace') and of John 15:25 ('without cause'). Here it means 'for nothing, to no purpose'. The word that speaks of grace's free gift becomes the charge: if righteousness comes through the law, the cross had no point. The Plain says 'for no reason' to bring out 'without cause'.

p: Paul's word means 'without understanding', not a slur on a people.
b: Anoētos means without understanding. Paul uses it in Romans 1:14 ('the wise and the foolish') and Titus 3:3 ('we ourselves were once foolish'), and Jesus uses the same word in Luke 24:25. Some argue that 'Galatians' favors the north, since only the Celtic people were ethnic Galatians; others reply that Roman provincials could be called by their province's name, as 'Philippians' for the people of Philippi. See the note at 1:2. The outburst fits the style of a speaker who has lost patience.

p: Paul half-jokes that someone has cast a spell, so strange is their behavior.
b: Baskainō means to harm by a look, to cast the evil eye. Belief in the evil eye was wide in the Mediterranean world: Plutarch, for example, discusses how a look could harm (Table Talk 5.7), and Jewish writers speak of the evil eye of envy (Sirach 14:8). Paul uses the word half in irony, as if the Galatians must have been bewitched to behave so oddly, and half in earnest: some power is at work (compare the 'elements of the world' of 4:3, 9, in part 4).

a: put on public display as the crucified one
p: The Greek can mean 'written up in public', like a notice posted in the marketplace.
b: Prographō can mean 'write beforehand' or 'write publicly', as on a notice or poster. 'In front of your eyes' puts it in a public place. Paul reminds them how vividly he had presented Christ crucified: not an idea but a notice posted in the square. The perfect tense 'crucified' stresses a lasting result: Christ remains the crucified one (1 Corinthians 1:23; 2:2). The cross was a shameful Roman death, the punishment of slaves and rebels, often carried out in public with the crime displayed (John 19:19-20).

t: How the Galatians received the Spirit
p: Paul's first proof is their own experience: they got the Spirit when they heard and believed.
b: Paul treats the Galatians' experience of the Spirit as undeniable. Acts shows the same pattern in Cornelius' household: "Peter was still saying these things when the Holy Spirit fell on everyone who was listening to the word" (Acts 10:44), before anyone was circumcised. What it looked like among the Galatians is not told; it probably included inspired speech, joy and healing (compare Acts 13:52; 1 Corinthians 12-14). Paul's argument is about how they got it: not by works of the law.

p: Hearing with faith, or the message that calls for faith? The Greek allows both.
b: Akoē can mean the act of hearing or what is heard (a report, a message), and pistis can mean faith or faithfulness. So: 'hearing with faith'; 'the message that calls for faith'; or 'what was heard', a report, as in Isaiah 53:1 ("Who has believed what we have heard?"), which Paul quotes in Romans 10:16-17. The Plain keeps the Greek shape so that each reader can see the options.

t: Start in the Spirit, finish in the flesh
p: 'Flesh' sets human effort, or the mark in the body, against the Spirit.
b: The verb 'finish' (epiteleō, bring to completion) is the verb of "the one who started a good work in you will go on completing it" (Philippians 1:6). Paul says the Galatians think the Spirit started them but the law and circumcision will complete them. A pun is likely: circumcision is a work done on the flesh (6:12-13). The sense of 'flesh' may be bodily (circumcision), moral weakness, or human strength; the Plain keeps the word so readers can follow it to 5:16-26.

p: The Greek verb usually means suffer, but it can also mean simply go through.
b: Paschō usually means to suffer, and persecution of the Galatians would fit the South Galatian view of Acts 13:50; 14:2-5 and 14:19: "They talked the crowds around, pelted Paul with stones and hauled him outside the town, believing he had died." The verb can also be neutral, 'experience', and the context (the gift of the Spirit and miracles) may favor 'did you experience so much' for good things. Most older commentators read 'suffer'; several recent ones favor 'experience'. Either way, the question is whether it was all for nothing.

p: The present tense shows these were still going on among the Galatians.
b: Dynameis is the usual word for miracles, deeds of power (1 Corinthians 12:10, 28). Acts says that Paul and Barnabas worked miracles in this region: "He backed up the word of his grace by granting that signs and wonders happen at their hands" (Acts 14:3), including a healing at Lystra (Acts 14:8-10). The present tense of 'gives' and 'does' implies continuing activity. Paul argues from their continuing experience: was it from works of the law or from the hearing of faith? The Galatians know the answer.

p: Paul begins the Abraham argument with the verse that says Abraham 'believed'.
b: This site's Plain of Genesis 15:6: "Abram put his trust in the LORD, and he reckoned it to him as righteousness." The Hebrew leaves open who 'reckoned'. Paul follows the Greek version, which has a passive ('it was reckoned'), and uses the verse in Romans 4:3, 9, 22 and James 2:23 uses it differently. Other Jewish texts read it with Abraham's testing: 1 Maccabees 2:52 asks, "Abraham: was he not found faithful in the test, and was it not reckoned to him as righteousness?" Paul keeps to the one verse, before circumcision (Genesis 17) and before the binding of Isaac (Genesis 22).
r: Genesis 15:6; Romans 4:3; Romans 4:9; Romans 4:22; James 2:23; 1 Maccabees 2:52; Genesis 17:10

p: Paul answers the question of who is in Abraham's family.
b: 'Sons' (huioi) is the legal word for heirs; 3:28 shows women are included. Genesis 17:5 says: "Abraham will be your name, because I have made you father of a multitude of nations." Views of how Gentile believers are Abraham's children: they become Abraham's family without becoming Jews, and Jewish believers remain Abraham's children by birth and by faith (Fredriksen, Gager, Nanos); they belong to the Israel of God as the new or true Israel (the older view of much of the patristic and Reformation tradition, for example Justin, Dialogue 11, which Nostra Aetate 4 and many Protestant writers now qualify with Romans 11:1, and which Paul does not state in so many words here); or Jew and Gentile are now one family (Wright).

a: All the nations will be blessed in you
p: A blend of two Genesis promises, which Paul calls the good news told ahead of time.
b: Paul's quotation blends Genesis 12:3 (this site's Plain: "All the clans of the earth will find blessing in you.") and Genesis 18:18 ("all the nations of the earth will find blessing in him"). The Hebrew verb can mean 'will be blessed' or 'will bless themselves' (Genesis 22:18). Paul reads it as a promise to the Gentiles. 'Told the good news ahead of time' is one Greek verb (proeuangelizomai), found only here in the New Testament: for Paul the good news of Christ is already inside the Abraham story. Sirach 44:21 also says the nations would be blessed through Abraham's offspring.

p: The Greek pistos can mean both; Jewish tradition heard 'faithful'.
b: Pistos means faithful or believing. The Plain says 'who believed', as the context of 3:6 suggests. Jewish tradition heard 'faithful': 1 Maccabees 2:52 and Sirach 44:20 say that Abraham was found faithful in testing, and 1 Maccabees ties it to Genesis 15:6. Hebrews 11 and James 2:21-23 read Abraham's life as faith in action, including the offering of Isaac. Paul stays with Genesis 15:6, which comes long before Isaac's binding.

t: Why are those 'from works of the law' under a curse?
p: Paul's logic is not spelled out; three ways of filling the gap.
b: Paul quotes a form of Deuteronomy 27:26, whose Plain reads: "A curse on anyone who does not make the words of this law stand by doing them!" He adds 'everyone', 'all' and 'the book of the law' (compare Deuteronomy 28:58; 29:20; 30:10). The missing step is debated. (1) No one keeps all the law, so everyone who relies on it is cursed (Luther, Calvin). (2) The law's curse fell on Israel as a nation in exile (Deuteronomy 27-30; Daniel 9:11-13) and was not lifted until Christ (Wright). (3) Those who use 'works of the law' as the badge that separates Israel from the nations have misread the law, which itself looks to faith (Dunn). Jewish readers point out that Deuteronomy 30 promises restoration after return, and the law has sacrifices for failure; Paul's argument runs against those provisions.

a: The righteous will live by faith
p: Paul reads the prophet's line as a statement about how the righteous live.
b: Habakkuk 2:4 is quoted three times in the New Testament (here, Romans 1:17 and Hebrews 10:38). This site's Plain of the Hebrew: "But the righteous will live by his faithfulness." The Greek Old Testament has 'by my faithfulness', and Paul has 'by faith' with no pronoun. Two debates: does 'by faith' go with 'the righteous' (the one who is righteous by faith will live) or with 'will live'? And is 'the Righteous One' a title for the Messiah (Hays; compare Acts 3:14)?

a: The one who does them will live by them
p: Paul sets the 'doing' of the law against faith; rabbis read the verse as a promise of life.
b: Leviticus 18:5 in this site's Plain: "If a human being does them, he will live by them." Paul sets it against faith, as in Romans 10:5-6. Jewish readers take the verse differently: 'live by them' means 'live, and not die', and the rabbis derived the rule that almost any commandment gives way to save a life (Babylonian Talmud, Yoma 85b; Sanhedrin 74a). Ezekiel 20:11, 13, 21 treats the verse as God's gift of life. Paul's use has been read as claiming that the law demands perfect doing (Luther), or that it describes a life of Torah-observance distinct from the life of faith.

p: A market word: to buy up, to buy out of ownership.
b: Exagorazō is a market word, 'to buy out'; Paul uses it again at 4:5. Who is 'us'? Most commentators think Jews, who were under the law's curse (3:10), with the Gentiles coming into the blessing in 3:14; others think 'us' is all believers or all humanity (Luther). To whom was the price paid? The fathers differed (Origen suggested the devil; Gregory of Nazianzus rejected that; Anselm in Cur Deus Homo framed it as satisfying God's honor); recent writers often avoid the question, since Paul does not ask it.

a: having become a curse for us
p: How did Christ become a curse, and what does 'for us' mean?
b: Christ's becoming 'a curse' is the mirror of 2 Corinthians 5:21 ('he made him to be sin for us'). Views: Christ bore the law's curse in the place of others (penal substitution; Luther, Calvin); he shared Israel's exile-curse as Israel's representative (Wright); he entered the place of the cursed to destroy it, the victory over death (an Orthodox emphasis). 'For us' (hyper hēmōn) can mean 'on our behalf' or 'in our place'. See the card.

p: Paul drops 'by God'; 'everyone' is in the Greek but not the Hebrew. A crucified Messiah was a scandal.
b: This site's Plain of Deuteronomy 21:23: "a man who is hanged is cursed by God." Paul leaves out 'by God'; 'everyone' (pas) is already in the Greek Deuteronomy, though the Hebrew has no such word. The law commanded burial the same day for the body of an executed criminal exposed on a tree. Justin's Jewish partner Trypho calls a crucified Messiah a problem (Dialogue 89-90). Paul accepts the objection and reverses it: the curse falls on Christ to free others.

p: Paul joins Abraham's blessing for the nations to the Spirit promised for the last days.
b: 'The blessing of Abraham' is the blessing of Genesis 12:3 for the nations. Paul then equates it with the promise of the Spirit, which the prophets set at the end of days: Isaiah 44:3 puts 'my Spirit' beside 'my blessing', and Joel 2:28 says, "I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh." Ezekiel 36:26-27 promises a new heart and God's Spirit. For Paul the Gentiles receive, through faith, what Israel was promised for the age to come. The Plain keeps 'promise of the Spirit' (the Spirit is the thing promised).

p: The Greek diatheke can mean covenant or a will; Paul's picture works with either.
b: Diathēkē is the Septuagint's regular word for Hebrew berit, 'covenant'. In everyday Greek it also meant a will, a legal instrument that could not be changed after it was ratified. Hebrews 9:16-17 plays on the 'will' sense. Paul's example works with either: once a human arrangement is ratified, no one cancels it or adds to it. His covenant in 3:15-17 is the covenant with Abraham, and some scholars hear 'will' in the picture. Lightfoot and Burton, though, take diathēkē in 3:15-17 as 'covenant' and not 'will': Lightfoot says the sense 'testament' is ill suited to the context and came in through the Latin version and Hebrews, and Burton says the 'inheritance' of 3:18 is no argument for 'will' in 3:17. The Plain uses 'covenant' as everywhere else.

p: Paul's argument hangs on a singular noun; scholars have found it brilliant, strained, or both.
b: In Genesis the Hebrew zera, 'seed', is a collective singular, like English 'offspring', and normally includes many (Genesis 13:15; 15:5; 17:7; 22:18). Paul says the text names 'one': Christ. Many readers have thought this a poor argument from grammar. Defenders offer: Paul reads the singular as one family summed up in one person (Wright; the 'one' of 3:16 is joined to the 'one' of 3:28); the offspring is the king who stands for Israel (2 Samuel 7:12); or this is the close-reading method of his time. The Plain uses 'offspring' to match Romans 4:13. In 3:29 the 'offspring' are all who belong to Christ, so the singular and the many are one.
r: Genesis 13:15; Genesis 15:5; Genesis 17:7; Genesis 22:18; 2 Samuel 7:12; Galatians 3:29

a: four hundred and thirty years later
p: Paul counts from Abraham's promise to Sinai, as the Greek Old Testament does.
b: Exodus 12:40 in this site's Plain: "The Israelites had lived in Egypt for a span of four hundred and thirty years." Paul counts from the promise to Abraham to the giving of the law, which agrees with the Greek Old Testament and the Samaritan Pentateuch, whose Exodus 12:40 says the 430 years include time in Canaan as well as Egypt. Genesis 15:13 gives four hundred years of oppression. The numbers differ in the sources, but Paul's point is the order: promise first, law much later.

p: The inheritance promised to Abraham was land; Paul and others enlarge it.
b: In the Old Testament the inheritance given to Abraham's offspring is the land (Genesis 15:7; 17:8: "To you and your offspring after you I will give the land where you now live as a foreigner"). Paul enlarges it: in Romans 4:13 the promise is that Abraham would 'inherit the world', in 3:29 the heirs are those who belong to Christ, and in 4:1-7 (part 4) they are God's children. Jewish writers also enlarged it: Sirach 44:21 speaks of an inheritance from sea to sea to the ends of the earth.

p: 'On account of transgressions' can be read at least five ways.
b: The Greek tōn parabaseōn charin is open. Views: (1) to make transgression known, defining sin (Romans 3:20; 4:15; 5:20; 7:7; Augustine, Luther); (2) to restrain sin until the offspring came (Calvin); (3) to provoke or increase sin so that it would show itself (Romans 5:20; 7:8-13); (4) to provide for dealing with sin through sacrifice and atonement while the people waited (some Jewish and Christian readers); (5) to gather Israel's sin in one place so that it could be dealt with in Christ (Wright). 'Until' shows the law was temporary.

p: In Jewish tradition angels at Sinai honored the law; Paul uses the tradition to show it came at second hand.
b: The Greek Old Testament of Deuteronomy 33:2 has 'angels with him' at Sinai (this site's Plain of the Hebrew has 'ten thousands of holy ones'). Psalm 68:17, Acts 7:38, 53 and Hebrews 2:2 also put angels at the giving of the law, and so does Jubilees 1:27-29, where the angel of the presence writes for Moses. Josephus has Herod say that 'we learned the finest of our doctrines and the holiest of our laws from messengers sent by God' (Antiquities 15.136). In Jewish tradition this was an honor. Paul uses the same tradition to say the law came 'through angels, by the hand of a mediator', where the promise came directly from God.
r: Deuteronomy 33:2; Psalm 68:17; Acts 7:38; Acts 7:53; Hebrews 2:2; Jubilees 1:27-29

a: by the hand of a mediator
p: 'By the hand of' is a Hebrew way of saying 'through'; the mediator is Moses.
b: 'By the hand of' is a Hebrew idiom for 'through' (Leviticus 26:46: through Moses). The Testament of Moses calls Moses 'the mediator of his covenant' (1:14; 3:12), and Philo calls him 'mediator and reconciler' (Life of Moses 2.166). Hebrews 8:6 and 9:15 call Jesus the mediator of a better covenant (compare 1 Timothy 2:5). Paul sets the mediated law against the direct promise in 3:20.

a: a mediator is not of one
t: The most puzzling verse in Galatians
p: Commentators have counted hundreds of readings; here are the main ones.
b: The Greek is only a few words and does not say what 'one' is. Main readings. (1) A mediator stands between two sides, so the law was a two-sided arrangement that depended on Israel keeping it, while the promise came from God alone (Lightfoot, Burton). (2) The law came by mediation, through angels and Moses, so it was less direct than the promise. Lightfoot says the number of interpretations of this verse 'is said to mount up to 250 or 300'.
orig: ὁ δὲ μεσίτης ἑνὸς οὐκ ἔστιν (ho de mesites henos ouk estin)

t: A law that could give life
p: The law promised life to the one who does it, but could not give it.
b: Paul's claim is that the law, which promised life to the one who does it (3:12), had no power to give it. The verb zōopoieō is the one used of God giving life to the dead (Romans 4:17; 8:11; 1 Corinthians 15:22). Paul does not deny that the law is good (Romans 7:12) or that it promised life; he says the life does not come from it, because of sin's hold (3:22; Romans 8:3). Jewish readers will hear a challenge to Torah as the tree of life (Proverbs 3:18; Baruch 4:1).

p: Scripture is the jailer here, and sin is a power.
b: The picture is of fish enclosed in a net or prisoners locked in. Scripture is the subject: what Scripture says (for example, Psalm 143:2; compare the catena of Romans 3:10-18) shuts everyone in. 'Sin' here is a power, as in Romans 5-7. In Romans 11:32 God 'shut up' all in disobedience so as to have mercy on all. The prison is temporary: 3:23 says 'until'.

t: 'Faith of Jesus Christ' at 3:22: the hardest place for 'faith in'
p: The Greek can mean faith in Christ or the faithfulness of Christ; here the verse already speaks of 'those who believe'.
b: The Greek is ek pisteōs Iēsou Christou. 'Faith in Jesus Christ' (objective genitive) is the Plain's reading, as at Romans 3:22 and Galatians 2:16, and is the reading of most English versions. 'The faithfulness of Jesus Christ' (subjective genitive) is argued by a number of recent scholars. Here the objective reading has a cost: the verse goes on 'to those who believe', so 'faith in Jesus Christ' makes the sentence say the same thing twice, while the other reading gives the two halves different subjects, his faithfulness and their believing. The verse also sits next to 3:23-25, where 'the faith' comes as an event, which some take to mean Christ's own faithfulness. The case for the objective reading rests chiefly on 2:16, 'we also believed in Christ Jesus', and on Paul's use of the verb 'believe'. A reader may follow either reading here without following it everywhere. See the variant entry and the topic page Faith in Christ or the Faithfulness of Christ?
orig: ἐκ πίστεως Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ (ek pisteos Iesou Christou)

a: kept under guard under the law
p: A guard can protect or imprison; Paul's words allow both.
b: Phroureō is to guard, as a garrison guards a city (2 Corinthians 11:32, where the governor guarded Damascus). Is the guard protective (keeping the child safe) or custodial (a jailer)? 'Locked up' sounds like prison, 'attendant' (3:24) like protection. Who is 'we'? Jews, held under Torah until the faith came, while Gentiles were outside (compare 4:3, 8); or everyone (Luther).

p: Faith 'came' like an event; some readers say 'the faith' is Christ's own faithfulness.
b: Faith 'came' and 'was revealed' as an event in time: with Christ a new age of faith began, though people believed before (Abraham, 3:6). J. Louis Martyn built his reading on the 'apocalypse' of 3:23, a coming and sending as in 4:4-6; others who read pistis Christou as Christ's faithfulness take 'the faith' as his faithfulness; others take it as the new era of faith in Christ. See the note at 2:16. The apocalyptic language ('revealed') matches 1:12, 16.

p: The King James 'schoolmaster' misleads: a paidagogos supervised a boy and was not his teacher.
b: In Greek and Roman households a paidagōgos was a trusted slave who watched over a boy from childhood to adolescence, took him to and from school and enforced good behavior. He was not the teacher. The KJV's 'schoolmaster' gave generations of readers the idea that the law taught people about Christ. English versions have 'guardian', 'custodian', 'tutor' or 'disciplinarian'; the Plain uses 'attendant' throughout (3:24-25 and these notes). The image shows the law as temporary and subordinate: needed while the boy was a minor, not in adult life (4:1-2). Positive readers stress protection and discipline; negative readers stress harshness. Plato's Lysis (208c) describes a boy ruled by a paidagogos.

p: The Greek 'eis' can mean 'until' (time) or 'toward' (aim).
b: Eis with the accusative can mean 'until' (time) or 'to, toward' (aim). The KJV's 'to bring us unto Christ' takes it as purpose: the law leads people to Christ by showing their need, a reading that Luther and Calvin favored. Most modern commentators take it as time ('up to the coming of Christ') because 3:25 says that when faith came, 'we are no longer under the attendant'. The Plain follows the time sense.

t: Is the law over for Jews too?
p: Does 'we are no longer under' mean the law ended for everyone, or only for Gentiles?
b: Views: the law's role as guardian ended for everyone in Christ, Jew and Gentile (the traditional Christian reading); it ended as a way to righteousness, though Jewish believers may continue to live by the Torah as a way of life (Messianic Jewish readings; Nanos); the 'we' under the attendant were Jews, and Paul does not say the law is over for Jews but only that Gentiles are not to be brought under it (Gager, Eisenbaum). Acts 21:20-24 shows James and the elders expecting Jewish believers to keep the law, and Paul agreeing to a vow: "They will see that you too walk in line with the law and keep it."

t: Sons of God: Israel's title, shared
p: Israel was called God's son; Paul says all believers are sons by faith.
b: Israel is called God's son (Exodus 4:22: "Israel is my son, my firstborn") and the Israelites 'sons of the living God' (Hosea 1:10). Paul says all believers, Jew or Gentile, are sons by faith. 'Sons' (huioi) is the legal term for heirs; it includes women, as the next verses show. Adoption into God's family comes in 4:5-7. 'Through faith in Christ Jesus' may be joined differently: 'in Christ Jesus you are all sons of God, through faith.'

t: Baptized into Christ and clothed with Christ
p: 'Into Christ' is Paul's phrase for what baptism does; 'put on' is the language of clothes.
b: 'Into Christ' is Paul's phrase for baptism's effect (Romans 6:3; 1 Corinthians 12:13). 'Put on Christ' uses the picture of clothing; the same verb appears in Romans 13:14 and Colossians 3:9-10 (the new self). The picture may come from Isaiah 61:10, and later writers describe new white garments after baptism. Wayne Meeks proposed that 3:26-28 is a baptismal formula Paul quotes, found also in 1 Corinthians 12:13 and Colossians 3:11. See the card.

p: Does Paul end the difference between Jew and Gentile, or only the division between them?
b: Paul does not say Jews become Gentiles or the reverse. Views. (1) Equal standing before God, with the distinctions continuing in social and ethnic life: Jewish believers remain Jews and Gentile believers remain Gentiles, one in Christ (many Catholic and Protestant interpreters). (2) The same, with Jewish Torah observance continuing for Jews and not required of Gentiles (Nanos, Gager, Eisenbaum; Messianic Jewish readings). (3) The distinction is dissolved into a universal human identity (Daniel Boyarin reads Paul as wanting a humanity made one, and says that Jewish difference is lost in the process). (4) The church is the new or true Israel, in which the old categories are taken up (the older view in much of the patristic and Reformation tradition, for example Justin, Dialogue 11); Nostra Aetate 4 and many Protestant writers now qualify it with Romans 11:1, holding that God has not rejected his people. The three pairs also appear in 1 Corinthians 12:13 and Colossians 3:11.

a: no slave and no free person
t: No slave and no free person
p: Paul does not call for abolishing slavery; readers have drawn very different conclusions.
b: A large part of the population of Roman cities were slaves. Paul does not call for abolition: in 1 Corinthians 7:21-24 he tells slaves who can gain freedom to use it, and in Philemon he asks Philemon to receive Onesimus back 'no longer as a slave but as a brother'. Later readers differ on what equality 'in Christ' requires in society: Gregory of Nyssa, in a homily on Ecclesiastes, condemned slavery outright; slaveholders in the American South appealed to other passages; abolitionists appealed to this one.

p: Paul changes his wording for the third pair, using the words of the creation story.
b: The first two pairs use 'neither... nor', but the third says 'male and female' (arsen kai thēly), the wording of Genesis 1:27 in the Greek Bible (this site's Plain: "male and female he created them"). Paul seems to hear the creation story: in Christ the new creation (6:15) restores what 'male and female' means. Meeks linked the formula with the myth of an original androgynous human. A rabbinic blessing has a man thank God each day for not making him a Gentile, a woman or an ignoramus (Babylonian Talmud, Menachot 43b, a teaching of Rabbi Meir; the Jerusalem Talmud, Berakhot 9:1, gives it to Rabbi Judah as 'Gentile, uncivilized person, woman'; 'slave' appears only in the discussion that follows in Menachot, where a rabbi proposes it in place of 'ignoramus'). These sources are later than Paul, and whether an earlier custom lies behind them is uncertain. A Greek saying that Hermippus told of Thales, and that others told of Socrates (Diogenes Laertius 1.33) thanks fortune for being a human and not a beast, a man and not a woman, a Greek and not a barbarian. Some read Paul's three pairs as an answer to sayings like these. The verse is central to debates about women in ministry. See the card.

p: The Greek 'one' is masculine, 'one person'; it echoes the 'one' offspring and the 'one' God.
b: The Greek heis is masculine: 'one man, one person'. It echoes 3:16 (the promise goes to 'one') and 3:20 ('God is one'). 'In Christ' is Paul's phrase for the shared sphere of believers. Not everyone agrees that 'one' abolishes every difference; 1 Corinthians 12:12-27 also describes a body with many parts.
orig: εἷς ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ (heis en Christo Iesou)

p: Verse 29 closes the circle opened in 3:16.
b: Verse 29 answers 3:16: the 'one' offspring is Christ, and those who belong to Christ are counted as Abraham's offspring. The promise therefore reaches Gentiles without circumcision, because they are 'in' the one to whom it was made. 'Heirs' (klēronomoi) leads into the inheritance language of 4:1-7. 'In line with the promise' translates kata epangelian, 'according to promise'.
